rv.q: If you are nervously venturing back into the West End and looking for something that illustrates the profound imaginative power of theatre, you really couldn’t do better than choose this bittersweet 1990s tale...
This charming show brings some much-needed silly delight.

In its best moments, Amelie leans into the whimsy and embraces full-on absurdity: an exquisite Elton John parody (an incredible impersonation from Caolan McCarthy) or a nightmare involving killer figs.

Nonetheless, much as I admire Amelie’s boho ensemble ethos, its undeniable physical zest, and the company’s determination (assisted by help from the Culture Recovery Fund) to open in the West End at this critical time, I wasn’t quite as bouleversé as I expected.
This production doesn't fix 'Amélie the Musical', but mon dieu it makes it fun.
And yet, like the story, the meandering melodies and wistful songs go nowhere.
This slice of Paris life comes alive.
This delightful, life affirming show is the perfect tonic to our gloomy, post-election, winter.
This musical is making a big impact.

cn.t: This charming musical adaptation of the beloved French film divides critics with its whimsy, but most find it enchanting. Audrey Brisson's performance wins praise, though some find the show overlong and exasperating.

vr.q: I really enjoyed it. I thought it was really dynamic, really funny, really expressive, really emotive.
